 Money for more SNAP caseworkers tied up in closeout budget talks 
 Political and bureaucratic challenges collide 
 Katie Lannan / 
 Nov 19, 2026 
 Thriving with care: Atrius Health helps patients and families do more of what they love. With connected care for adults and children at nearly 30 locations across eastern Massachusetts, Atrius Health primary care providers and specialists work together to help you live well. Find a provider at atriushealth.org . 
 It’s not the gas tax, social media rules, public records or how, precisely, to go about lowering energy bills and making it easier to see a primary care provider.  
 But in the mix with all those debates still swirling, there’s at least one spot where the House , Senate and Gov. Maura Healey are all on the same page: Massachusetts, staring down the barrel of major changes to the SNAP program, needs more caseworkers to help people access food benefits and stay enrolled. 
 Leran Minc , Project Bread's director of public policy, says a lack of caseworkers is part of an "access crisis."  
 Many people who dial the Department of Transitional Assistance trying to speak to caseworkers get a message telling them the call volume is too high, Minc said.  
 A class action suit, filed on behalf of families whose SNAP benefits were terminated or decreased after they couldn't reach a caseworker, put a number on the automatic disconnections: 74 to 81% on average in the first half of this  year. 
 "Maybe eventually they'll get through, or they have to make their way to a DTA office, which there's not many of those, and sometimes even there they may be waiting a long time and may not get the help they need," Minc said.  
 The One Big Beautiful Bill Act President Trump signed last year expanded SNAP's work requirements and made changes to how the food assistance program is funded, so state governments pick up a bigger share while the federal government pulls back. 
 As of last month, states are paying more of SNAP's administrative costs while federal funding dropped, and another change looms. Starting next October, states would need to cover part of the food benefit costs, too, if their error rates are above 6% — which Massachusetts' was in fiscal 2025 . 
 In a supplemental budget to close the books on the last fiscal year, Healey requested extra money to support SNAP recipients, including nearly $15 million for technology and staff investments at the DTA to reduce the state's payment-error rate in line with the guidelines. Another $26.6 million would boost the agency's funding to hire and pay caseworkers. 
 The House and Senate not only met but exceeded Healey's ask, each upping the caseworker money to $54.5 million in passing their versions of the spending bill. That amount, lawmakers and advocates say, would support 200 new caseworkers. 
 Minc said that will make a "significant difference," though it's tough to quantify how many additional caseworkers the department needs. That's in part because the new federal rules translate to longer eligibility interviews, more documents and more phone calls. 
 "We really need to make sure not only do we get the phones answered and documents processed and all the basics of government working smoothly, we need to do it in a way that people who may have fallen off a program but are still struggling are able to think, 'Yes, it is worth it for me to apply again and to engage with state government and to be able to get my benefits,'" Minc said. 
 So that’s the bureaucratic challenge. But first comes the political one. 
 How soon the DTA can get the money depends on how long it takes for the House and Senate to agree on everything else the two branches wrapped up in their closeout budgets, from more than $2 billion in total spending to policy pieces limiting AI in political ads or codifying rules for simpler subscription cancellations. 
 The House and Senate, coincidentally, took their final votes on last year's closeout budget one year ago today. If you placed a bet on when this year's gets done, I hope you took the over. Loop me in on any of your legislative wagers: [email protected] .
